newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's foreign minister backs NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Austria's foreign minister backs NATO entry.

text.p: Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel on Thursday threw his full weight behind membership of the NATO Western military alliance, saying neutral Austria had to move with the times.
In his most unequivocal comment so far on NATO entry, Schuessel told Austria's upper house of parliament:
"The time is ripe for fully justified membership of NATO."

Schuessel, leader of the conservative People's Party, has usually been more circumspect on the NATO issue to avoid friction with his dominant Social Democrat coalition partners, who mostly oppose any move to join the 16-nation alliance.

But Schuessel now appears intent on following the trail set by Defence Minister Werner Fasslabend, also a conservative, who said last week that Austria had to join a military pact if it wanted a voice in Europe's future security.
"We should now be able to make a decision on joining (NATO) freely and without any influence," Schuessel said.

During the Cold War, the Soviet Union made clear Austria had to remain neutral and only pulled its troops out of the country in 1955 on condition that neutrality was enshrined in the Austrian constitution.
Austria, annexed by Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler in 1938, was occupied by Russia in 1945 with the other World War Two victors, the United States, France and Britain.

On a key visit to Vienna last year, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told government leaders that while the Kremlin preferred Austria to remain neutral, it would no longer oppose the country joining a military alliance.

Schuessel told the upper house that choosing neutrality was right in 1955, but that the political landscape had altered radically since 1989 with the collapse of communism in Austria's neighbours in Eastern Europe.

"We have got to face the fact that the times are changing," said Schuessel, whose conservatives are trying to push the issue to the top of the government agenda while the Social Democrats remain largely silent.

He called for a full, open debate on NATO membership but repeated his opposition to holding a national referendum just a day after President Thomas Klestil said the nation of eight million should decide on the issue through a plebiscite.
"NATO membership is such a crucial question for our country, that it is justifiable to consider asking the nation," Klestil told the daily Kurier.

Schuessel knows that if the issue ever went to parliament for a decision, his conservatives would probably be able to muster a majority in favour of membership with the backing of the fervent pro-NATO far-right Freedom Party and the liberals.
But recent opinion polls suggest a majority of Austrian citizens, already disillusioned with membership of the European Union, would reject NATO entry.
Schuessel still clings to the belief that Austria might be able to join NATO and retain some measure of neutrality -- a status unlikely to be accepted by other NATO members.
